messages.author: ec32e5a92a275a89
messages.subject: Projects coming in
parts:
We now have 18 project proposals. There are several "multiplets", that is, projects
looking at the same base idea. We can, I believe, actually have more than one project
working on the same ideas, especially if the students are all strong candidates. However,
we may want to work out some way to avoid duplication of effort in such cases.

I welcome ideas about how to do this if we get, as I suspect we may, such multiple strong
submissions.

We also have some of us listed as mentors for multiple projects. That's OK too, but
Claudia and I did intend to have a list of alternates. Last year I really owed a lot to
some folk who helped me mentor a student, so I encourage involvement of "unofficial"
mentors. They also provide a fall-back in case of unforeseen events.

Tomorrow I'll be off-line (on airplanes all day), so non-reply does not mean I'm ignoring
people then.

Scoring of projects will occur over the next couple of weeks. A couple of ours have scores
already, though I feel it may be a good idea to wait until the submissions are frozen on
April 8 (Fri) so scores are for complete submissions.

Melange has been updated again. Seems to be sending me and possibly others lots of
"notification" emails. Hitting "enter" seems to generate such. Sorry to those of you who
have received these rather meaningless emails.

Best,

John Nash

If a mentor wants to have multiple students working on the same
project they will really need to make strong case for it.

I've just skimmed through a number of the proposals, and I'd urge
mentors to remember that non-experts will be reviewing the proposals
too. I don't want to have to read four different references to figure
out what the student is proposing. It would also be helpful if every
proposal included a short blurb describing why (in the student's
words) the project is important to the R community, and how it
compares to existing approaches.

messages.author: ec32e5a92a275a89
messages.subject: Re: Projects coming in
parts:
Some trouble sending this. Trying again.

Actually I'm not sure "want" to have multiple students is the right word. As admin and
mentor, at this stage before we score proposals
I don't feel it is my place to refuse proposals. I prefer if it works out that there is
one proposal for each good suggestion. Students
do however have the option to submit proposals, and we shouldn't shut them out because
there is already one there.

However, we may well get a couple of strong candidates for a single proposal that are
"stronger" than singlets.
In such a case, what is our position as representatives of R? My own feeling is that we
should propose that two
strong candidates be funded rather than a couple of singlet proposals with weaker candidates.

It's not a simple situation, and it is complicated in my own case that I am mentoring for
one of our colleagues
who may be better qualified than I to mentor but may for particular reasons be unable to
be official mentor.

Hadley makes a point that students should make a strong justification for their project
that is comprehensible to non-specialists.

Best, JN

> Actually I'm not sure "want" to have multiple students is the right word. As admin and

> strong candidates be funded rather than a couple of singlet proposals with weaker candidates.

> It's not a simple situation, and it is complicated in my own case that I am mentoring for

> who may be better qualified than I to mentor but may for particular reasons be unable to
> be official mentor.

I generally agree that two strong candidates are better than a mediocre
proposal.

I have two reasonably strong proposals that overlap only slightly, but
would both extend the same set of R packages. I've suggested to both
students that they strengthen the non-overlapping parts of their
applications.

To the degree that we want to get enduring contributions to the body of
R package code, I think this general approach makes sense: split the
work, to the degree possible, into non-overlapping functionality.

Google takes a somewhat looser view, some of the documents I've read
suggest that multiple 'competing' or 'alternate' implementations of the
same functionality may be desirable in some cases.

If the proposals are really overlapping, then we probably need to
consider whether one of the overlapping proposals should be ranked lower
than the other, in the case that Google does not fund all the students
that we would like to accept.

My .02,

- Brian
